parts.asked: Do you want to tell me a little bit about yourself?
parts.text: To answer your question, I started as a teacher in DC, went to Excel Academy up in Boston, where we were starting a turnaround. I was part of the leadership team there that led culture operations and student services. We had a great team, and we were able to take that school from 270th in the state to number one and actually earned National Charter School of the Year. And in that, we got a lot of visitors. [[slow]]

parts.asked: (Your background answer to Gillian. Used here for the consulting part, because the Dan version has the health reason in it.)
parts.text: I then was able to launch a consulting practice. We had a lot of visitors at Excel. as you know happens in the charter community. And a lot of folks wanted to figure out what you know, how to bring what we were doing to their schools. And so I consulted With KIPP, Achievement First, Uncommon, all the Northeast charters, and some across the country.

… And I got to walk into 100 different schools, find and fix problems, help people improve systems, help each principal set their goals and figure out how to meet them. Yeah. So I'd meet them where they are, chaotic to stable. Do they need to go stable to functional, functional to rigorous? And this was with the big charters at the time in the Northeast and some around the country.
[[trim]] … When I was there at Excel, I needed a tool for some behavior and attendance incentive and communication tracking. So I started an Excel spreadsheet, which I later grew into DeansList. …

After consulting for a while, I found a client I was really keen on called Collegiate down in New Orleans. They have a true all-means-all mission. And I was really impressed to see how they had done special education at such true deep levels. And while they had that ambition, they were still trying to figure out could they be a super high expectations and a high support organization. They had a bunch of success at their first site, but they scaled, didn't work. My job as a consultant was to come down and assess whether or not the principal running their largest high school could do the job, a last-ditch effort. Loved the work. We were able to be successful in that. That led into a chief culture position that I was able to do while maintaining a very small consulting portfolio. So went down to New Orleans, moved my life down there, went all in, really learned a lot, enjoyed working as part of that team. [[slow]]

The plan was always to move back to New York. It wasn't necessarily my plan, but it was my wife's plan since she's from New York, and that's where we had met. So I was able to take a client called Brooklyn Lab that I had. They needed a transition superintendent to help them through renewal as well as being transferred over to a new ownership. The executive director and founder was trying to exit. So long story short, I took that on, did that for about a year and a half, built a remote school, led through COVID, got the schools through both those renewals. And that wasn't super easy, because of some of the knots and tangles that existed there. I'm happy to go more into that.

But then after that, we went to the KIPP Foundation where I just came from. That's the national support arm. We were working to get our 28 wonderful, but very independent regions into a degree of alignment on national high school strategy and then hand it back to the regional teams, which is where it lives now. So it's a two-year design and hand-back role.

Right now, what I'm doing, which is something I think is really cool, is I am talking to the principals I know, finding where they need help with efficiency and effectiveness, what their problems are, and figuring out how I can build them custom tools, workflows, apps, solutions using AI to build the specific solutions that they need …

[[pause]] But really, at the end of the day, the happiest I've ever been is in a midsize growing charter network that has wildly outsized ambition and is full of smart, aspirationally aligned folks. And my read is that you all might be that place and that this role just really spoke to me as a perfect blend of what I've done, what I want to do, and where I might want to be. So that's why I'm here.

q: How do you manage principals? The good principal who needs to get to great?
hook: Clothes, not skin · support hat 99% · side of the street clean · shoulder to shoulder → Carver
why: Paola's job. Dan asked exactly this, and the answer had no proof.
frame: The playbook I've developed over time, by doing it wrong and then eventually doing it better, comes down to four things.

parts.asked: What's the common piece of feedback you give the principal who is pretty good but needs to go to great?
parts.text: I would say that the playbook that I have developed over time by doing it wrong and then eventually doing it better and then doing it well a few times at least is I think the first thing is we have to separate someone's performance from their identity. And I talk about using your identity not as your skin, but your identity as a principal is the clothes that you wear, not the skin that you're in. And helping them separate this idea that there are things that make you who you are that are irreplaceable and that nothing about those should change. There are, however, also ways in which we can build on those strengths. And by aligning on what the key problems or opportunities are, we can focus on improving those without undercutting either who you are, the strengths you bring, or attacking your personal identity. So that's number one. Number two is getting clear on support versus evaluation. 99% of the time, I'm wearing my support hat. My success is entirely a function of your success. And so that when it comes time to evaluate, number one, nothing is a surprise. And number two, I've helped you along the way so that your review is wildly positive. The third thing is my side of the street needs to be totally clean above reproach. I need to be clear. I need to follow through. I need to be the model for reliability, for clarity and communication. And number four, doing the work alongside them. I think so often it's easy for folks, especially that have been doing it for a while, to say, "Even if I respect you, even if I think you're great, you don't really get it, or you don't get it at the level that I'm currently experiencing it." And that's true. And I think with most conversations with smart people, acknowledging that their perspective is entirely valid is both necessary and important. Also, there are ways in which you can dive in, do the work alongside them, and really go shoulder to shoulder with them. And I'll close with this. Mandate authority is almost worthless in these settings. I mean, sure, you're the person's boss. Sure, you can say we are or aren't doing certain things, and you need to. However, for the people that we want to keep, like you said, the people who are innovative, who are strong, who bring their whole selves, we need to convince them through the quality of our ideas and our actions and through the data on what directions and changes need to be made. And so we need to be able to lead through influence and through modeling and completely let go of any hierarchical sense of mandate authority.

say: End on Carver instead of "completely let go of any hierarchical sense of mandate authority": I was brought in to assess whether the principal of their largest high school could do the job. Three years later the school had doubled, and he was Louisiana Principal of the Year. He runs the network now.
land: Say the Carver result, then stop.
avoid: Ending on the principle. Going past 2 minutes.
bul: 1. Performance is not identity: clothes, not skin
2. Support vs. evaluation: support hat 99%, nothing is a surprise
3. My side of the street clean, above reproach
4. Shoulder to shoulder; their perspective is valid
Mandate authority is almost worthless
End on Carver

q: What should high school be? What would you rethink?
hook: Not middle school with the dials turned · same spine, dressed different · 50/25/25
why: Dan's biggest open problem, and he said "I love that idea." Last time you opened with "I wish I had the answer."
frame: High school can't be like middle school just with a couple of dials turned.

parts.asked: Where are high schools getting it right, and where does there need to be a complete structural rethinking?
parts.text: … We get into a lot of and I think that's what a lot of folks have done. Because like you said, some of the things wear off, some of the things that compelled students in middle school either don't hold for different reasons. Number two, we can't overcorrect and we can't undercorrect on our systems and our structures. When we try and go too far and we don't have any systems, students are looking left and looking right and being like, "Do you even have it together? What is going on? This is not what I signed up for." At the same time, if we don't evolve them in strategic ways, you guys are treating me like I'm still in middle school. And so I would think about it the way I think about my classroom, which is I'm starting a new school year. It's a new group of students. I'm teaching something different. What is it that I did in the past that worked that I need to replicate for this group? And I think it would be about defining a wholly different identity, making sure that this was one that was resonant with students and that we had a spine, a skeleton of the same values, but we dressed it entirely different. And I don't mean dress in terms of faking or putting on just bells and whistles. What I simply mean to say is our values are still our values. But how they show up and what they look like and what the experience of a student is going to be does need to be fundamentally different.

[[trim]] I would ideally have us start at the end of seventh grade and begin a transition towards independence. In eighth grade, one of the things we did at Excel and we started to do at collegiate was run the second semester of each of those years as intentional transition points where we said, "We're going to remove the seating chart. Before we do that, we're going to teach you why it existed, what are the choices people are making, what does it look like to choose the seat?" And then we let kids fail. Sorry, I should say, we let kids choose their own seat. Some of them did well, some of them didn't. And we didn't immediately jump in and say, "Okay, fine. Here's where you sit." We let it run and we let kids sit with and see what the outcome, how the outcome of that two-weeks grading cycle, how it changed. And we reflected with them and gave them another opportunity, again, to choose. And we did three to four cycles of that for multiple discrete skills such that we were taking all of our we were taking, let's say, 40% of our 50% of our systems that were meant as placeholders or substitutes for the real skill, the student choice, the student understanding of why. So this is the org system. This is office hours and tutoring, student materials, late homework, or late work policy. And we systematically took those back, gave, like I said, the front-end instruction, the opportunity to try it out, and multiple cycles of that. And I think that's where I would want to start doing that in eighth grade so that we could do that in high school. And I think it's hard, though, because if you start that exact strategy in high school, are we really willing to say to students that we're going to take the first semester of their year and let things slide or let things slip? Because that's obviously highly problematic. So I think what I would try and do is find a way to apply some of that same logic.

[[slow]] I would take a look at my middle school plays. I would say, "Which 25% of these no longer make sense? Or what are the 50 that are core we're going to keep? What are the 25% that don't make sense anymore or we don't need them? And then what are the 25% that we are going to intentionally do pretty quick gradual release with instruction and reflection as a primary starting point?" All built around aiming at a different identity and an endpoint rather than we did in middle school because middle school is obviously focused on the high school portion of it. So then we have to focus on the lives of unlimited opportunity and what that means to a scholar in terms of what they need to do to advance and arrive at the right place.

q: Beyond systems: culture and student ownership
hook: Cool to be smart · ownership that isn't surfacey · "it's my school"
why: Dan's follow-up question. It shows the culture side is academic identity, not pizza parties.
frame: Two corners made all the difference at Excel.

parts.asked: Beyond seating charts, what other specific things would you change about high school?
parts.text: It sounds like you're in a place that where I think we got to a place at Excel where things were functional, things were academically focused, things were working. Were they perfect? No, of course not. But were they functional? Yes. And one of the corners that we turned two corners that made all the difference. One was what was teacher doing bell to bell in terms of rigor and instruction that gave us a sense of purpose and built an academic identity of cool to be smart, cool to work hard, and driving that as whereas in middle school, it might have been more focused on incentives and rewards or team. We switched it to a little bit more of an individual and more of an academic rigorous folk. It's not fun because it's fun. It's fun because it's challenging. And so building a true academic scholarly identity is number one. And number two, we always talk about student ownership over culture and over the school. And oftentimes, those end up being thin and surfacey. And so what I would do, I believe, would be something we did at Excel, which is to develop a lot of genuine student groups that play a key role, not just in the planning of the dance or the student council, but that are actually operating within the school day to help the school operate, to build the students who are involved in it to build their place and identity, but also so other students could see that this is the school that both trusts, empowers students, and those students are actually doing the thing incredibly well. So we'd have an honor council, right? And that honor council would be entirely responsible for within limits, of course, but doing a bit of investigation, evaluation around honor code violations, making recommendations. And we would put them front and center in terms of as much as we could from a legal and reasonable parent perspective, putting them in the position of understanding, deciding, and supporting scholars who are struggling. We would have groups that are intentionally owning and planning some of our joy factor or student events. All of these would be undergirded by our values. So not only would the group of the ninth-grade events committee be planning the dance, they'd be hyping the dance, they'd also attach a service commitment to it or a canned food drive to it. And they would be the ones making the announcements. They would be the one speaking and doing all of the things that oftentimes we have adults still do, even though behind the scenes, students are doing it. So it's really moving kids from supporting the school from an aspirational idea to action, but also to a level of doing it actually quite publicly. And that is where in a high school of 150 students, first year, 150 students per grade, you can get it so that more than a third of those students at any given time is in a meaningful group like this. And so they're part of one, and then they're seeing three to four others. And that's how we really get students to get that feeling of not only is this high school and it's different, it's also my school. And so we have this we build this identity of belonging such that when students are joining I mean, one of the big groups we would do, and I'll leave it at this, is our orientation leaders. We would have sophomores and juniors leading our freshman orientation, 50% of it, right? We would help prep them. We would help we'd spend a lot of time getting them to be incredibly good at this. We'd record a lot of video so that we could show what it looks like. But we would, as adults, be saying a whole lot less and helping our students say a whole lot more.

parts.asked: Compare Excel to KIPP. What makes scale so hard for so many charters?
parts.text: … Now, in contrast that with Excel, where we had playbooks for everything, we were unapologetic about the adult culture values, the way in which we did things, and we replicated not quite as cloning. I don't use huge, but the principal who started our second school and then our third school inherited 95% of the play was exactly the same. We wanted to maintain an opportunity for innovation because we recognized that innovation, one, you don't get to keep the right talent if you don't allow for some of that. And two, that's the laboratory where all the other schools can get better because we're trying something new. So fundamentally, we were clear on who we were. We were unapologetic about growing meant starting from a proven starting point and growing at a pace such that we could maintain the level of talent that we needed to do that incredibly well. And yeah, at the end of the day, our philosophy was we are here to build dynasties, to create radical transformations so students could live lives of unlimited opportunities. …

But the way in which we grow with quality is starting from a solid foundation of what we know that works. q: An initiative you led from design through implementation across schools
hook: Data was there, nobody could use it · one button, a report per teacher · present but obscured → right in front of them
why: Your strongest scaling story. DREAM's recruiter called it "absolutely incredible."
frame: The academic health data transparency work.

parts.src: DREAM screen with Donna Choi Ellis, 08/17
parts.asked: Can you share one specific initiative or pilot you've led from design through implementation across multiple schools?
parts.text: The Academic health data transparency work that was a subset of our larger academic health work so I'll I'll set the scene a little bit. Every school on our network had grade books, they had tons of data, All of that data was in these large CSV files and Excel files. and While it was accessible or while it was there, people couldn't really use it. [[pause]] I went all in on Using Claude Code to build A Python script that parsed out these huge data sets and with the push of a button created individualized teacher reports Telling them, you know, here are the students of concern, the assignments of concern. Here's where you don't have enough of a certain type of assessment. Here's where, you know, you're Your grades seem to be skewing. So we got people weekly high quality personalized data that we were able to compare to a standard. We did the same thing for students.

parts.src: DREAM screen with Donna Choi Ellis, 08/17
parts.text: I designed this for one particular school, rolled it out at that school, and then we took it across the country. And so, We built these reports through the AI. Then we created a regular meeting cadence We created a team at the school I was looking into these things and was leading the work on the ground.
